# Draft:Edward London (gunmaker)

----
Edward London was a British gunmaker active in the City of London during the mid-19th century. He operated workshops along London Wall, an area historically associated with specialist crafts and trades, including the manufacture of firearms.
Biography
Records held by the Pitt Rivers Museum list Edward London as working at 50 London Wall between 1826 and 1827, before relocating to 51 London Wall from 1828 onwards. He is recorded at this latter address until at least 1866, indicating a prolonged period of activity within the London gun trade.
An insurance policy issued by the Sun Fire Office in 1838 records “Edward London, gun maker” at 51 London Wall, confirming his operation as a registered firearms manufacturer at that address during the early Victorian period.
The 1841 census lists an individual named Edward London employed as a gunmaker at 51 London Wall, supporting the continuity of workshop use during this period.
Edward London also appears in legal records. In 1849, he was called as a witness during the trial of John Howe at the Old Bailey, where he examined a pistol connected with the case, demonstrating his recognised expertise in firearms.
Firearms bearing the name Edward London are known to survive in private collections and museum holdings, reflecting his participation in London’s 19th-century gun-making industry.
